Q: How to display date as YYYYMMDD_HH24 using Solaris shell command? A:

you can use

date -u +'%Y-%m-%d-%H'

Q: Check if current .NET version is still supported in C# A:

It is not clear to me if you have multiple applications, where some still target .net 4.5, and have not been updated for a long time. Or if you are talking about a single application that have multiple versions, where some older versions still target 4.5.

If you have old applications that still need support you should have time allocated for maintaining any applications you support. You might get away deferring any maintenance until someone complains, but as soon as any work needs to be done the first step should be to apply any deferred maintenance, like updating dependencies, make sure it runs in your development environment etc.

If you have multiple versions of the same application in use, just provide updates for the latest version, or possibly a few major versions if there are incompatibilities that cannot be solved. This requires that the update process is reasonably simple, and that might require some effort in itself.

I'm assuming in both cases that this is some internal tool and not software for sale. If you are selling software you may need to consider legal liabilities. If you rely on unsupported third party components it will likely be much harder to avoid liability if something where to happen.

I'm also assuming the application is not security sensitive in any way, if it is you need to be proactive with updating it.

Q: Simple way to measure cell execution time in ipython notebook A:

Using datetime.datetime.now() is a simpler and more reliable way, in my opinion, to measure execution time.

You just need to save the start time and the end time for the piece of code whose execution time you want to measure, and proceed to calculate the difference between the values:

import datetime

start_time = datetime.datetime.now()

#place your code here

end_time = datetime.datetime.now()

elapsed_time = end_time - start_time

When you subtract two datetime objects you get a timedelta object, given in seconds and microseconds by default:

datetime.timedelta(seconds=3, microseconds=293745)

Therefore, you just need to print the elapsed time as you wish:

print(f'Cell ran in {elapsed_time}.')
print('Cell ran in ' + str(elapsed_time.seconds) + ' seconds.')
print('Cell ran in ' + str(elapsed_time.seconds) + ' seconds and ' + str(elapsed_time.microseconds) + ' microseconds.')

#Output:
Cell ran in 0:00:03.293745.
Cell ran in 3 seconds.
Cell ran in 3 seconds and 293745 microseconds.

In case you're working with minutes or hours long processes, you can divide the resulting seconds by 60 etc.

Q: gcc: how to only trace specific functions calls A:

If you want to trace specific function names, there is only one approach gives you direct control by name:

Use -finstrument-functions + a filter inside __cyg_profile_func_enter

This is the only practical GCC-supported method that lets you select functions by name at runtime.

GCC itself does not provide:

  • X __attribute__((instrument_function))
  • X a "positive" include list option
  • X name-based instrumentation at compile time

So filtering must happen inside the profiling hook.

How It Works

Compile with:

gcc -finstrument-functions your_program.c -ldl

Then implement:

#define _GNU_SOURCE
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <dlfcn.h>

void __attribute__((no_instrument_function))
__cyg_profile_func_enter(void *this_fn, void *call_site)
{
    Dl_info info;

    if (dladdr(this_fn, &info) && info.dli_sname) {
        if (strcmp(info.dli_sname, "target_func1") == 0 ||
            strcmp(info.dli_sname, "target_func2") == 0)
        {
            printf("Entering %s\n", info.dli_sname);
        }
    }
}

void __attribute__((no_instrument_function))
__cyg_profile_func_exit(void *this_fn, void *call_site)
{
}

The following methods fails to select by function name:

  • -pg
  • -mfentry
  • -finstrument-functions alone
  • Separate compilation units

Only the filtering approach gives you true name-based selection.

Important Notes

Compile with -rdynamic if symbols are missing:

gcc -finstrument-functions -rdynamic -ldl ...

Always mark the profiling functions:

__attribute__((no_instrument_function))

or you'll recurse infinitely.

For performance,

  • precompute a hash table of allowed names
  • Avoid repeated strcmp
  • Avoid heavy I/O inside the hook

Q: Is there a way In Android to listen to Audio Volume Changes only? A:

// Source - https://stackoverflow.com/a/78698328

// Posted by Robyer

// Retrieved 2026-02-20, License - CC BY-SA 4.0

String[] streamNames = {

    "volume_system_speaker",

    "volume_system_earpiece",

    "volume_notification_speaker",

    "volume_notification_earpiece",

    "volume_ring_speaker",

    "volume_ring_earpiece",

    "volume_music_speaker",

    "volume_music_earpiece",

};

for (String name : streamNames) {

Uri uri = Settings.System.getUriFor(name);

contentResolver.registerContentObserver(uri, false, myObserver);

}
